name: Platysma Botox (Nefertiti lift)

card.summary: Botulinum toxin injected along the jawline and neck bands to soften platysmal cords and sharpen the lower-face contour; described in published case series and small trials, with temporary, modest results.
card.aka: Nefertiti lift, platysma Botox, neck Botox, jawline Botox
card.note: Effects are temporary (Grokipedia gives three to four months) and the procedure is described as suiting mild to moderate neck aging rather than severe laxity.

quick.overview:
Platysma Botox, popularly called the Nefertiti lift, is a non-surgical injection of botulinum toxin into the platysma muscle, the thin muscle sheet of the front of the neck, and along the lower border of the jaw. It aims to soften vertical neck bands and give a subtle lift and more defined jawline.

It was described in 2007 by a Swiss dermatologist, Phillip M. Levy, in a paper based on 130 patients. Later clinical studies in plastic surgery journals have examined it, including small trials comparing it with other injection patterns.
quick.mechanism: The platysma runs from the upper chest to the lower jaw and pulls the lower face and mouth corners downward when it contracts. Botulinum toxin weakens the muscle, which proponents say reduces the downward pull on the jawline and relaxes visible bands.
quick.risks: Published descriptions treat the procedure as minimally invasive with temporary effects that fade after a few months and need repeat sessions. Possible effects of neck toxin injections generally include bruising and weakness of neighbouring muscles; results are described as subtle compared with surgical platysmaplasty. It is clinician-administered and not specific to looksmaxxing.

lead: The Nefertiti lift is a non-surgical cosmetic procedure in which botulinum toxin type A is injected into the platysma muscle, including vertical neck bands and the lower border of the mandible, to relax the muscle and reduce its downward pull on the lower face.[1][2] It aims to soften platysmal bands and produce a subtle lift and sharper definition of the jawline.[1]

The technique takes its name from the ancient Egyptian queen Nefertiti, whose bust is admired for its elongated neck and defined jaw. Swiss dermatologist Phillip M. Levy described it in the Journal of Cosmetic and Laser Therapy in 2007, reporting experience with 130 patients treated between November 2006 and April 2007.[1]

Later studies have examined it clinically. A 2017 study injected abobotulinumtoxinA along the mandibular border and platysmal bands and examined which patients respond,[3] and a 2018 crossover study compared the microbotox technique with the Nefertiti lift.[4] A 2026 split-face study in The Laryngoscope evaluates its effect on jawline contour.[5] Grokipedia describes the effects as temporary and subtle, lasting around three to four months, and best suited to mild to moderate neck aging rather than severe laxity.[1]

paras: The platysma is a thin, broad superficial muscle covering the front of the neck. It arises from the fascia over the upper chest and shoulder and inserts at the lower jaw, the skin of the cheek and lower lip, and the mouth corner, and it is supplied by the cervical branch of the facial nerve.[6] When it contracts it wrinkles the neck skin obliquely and can depress the lower jaw and lip.[6]

Vertical platysmal bands become more noticeable with age and can be worsened by weightlifting or facelift surgery.[6] Botulinum toxin is listed among interventions alongside conservative management and platysmaplasty, used when bands do not improve with time.[6] A textbook-style chapter describes three applications: sharpening the jawline with the Nefertiti lift, treating anterior neck bands and softening necklace lines.[7]

Levy's 2007 article presented the Nefertiti lift as a new technique for re-contouring the jawline, noting that earlier reports of jawline effects had come as a side effect of platysmal band treatment.[2] A 2009 French paper described injection techniques in the lower and middle face, neck and decollete including the Nefertiti lift.[8] Grokipedia states the procedure had become a staple in aesthetic clinics by the early 2010s, particularly in Europe and the United States.[1]

A 2017 study aimed at assessing efficacy and redefining patient selection injected the mandibular border and platysmal bands with abobotulinumtoxinA and used standardised before-and-after assessment of lower face and neck components.[3] A 2018 crossover study in patients previously treated with the Nefertiti lift compared the microbotox technique, which injects microdroplets into the dermis, with it.[4] Consensus and review papers describe neurotoxin use for jawline contouring, platysma bands and necklace lines.[7][9][10] Grokipedia says results are subtle and temporary and do not match surgery for severe laxity.[1]

The procedure is described as minimally invasive, but detailed adverse-event rates have not been published. Botulinum toxin injection near the neck carries the general risk of weakness in neighbouring muscles; the platysma contributes to lowering the lip and jaw.[6] Treatment effects wear off and repeat sessions are needed.[1]

The platysma is a thin, broad sheet of muscle lying just under the skin of the neck. It arises from fascia over the upper chest and shoulder, runs up across the collarbone, and its fibres insert along the lower edge of the jaw and into skin and tissue around the lower face and mouth corners. It is supplied by the cervical branch of the facial nerve. [6]

When it contracts it wrinkles the neck skin and pulls the corners of the mouth and lower lip downward, as in a frown. With age the muscle can thin and shorten, and the vertical cords that stand out at the front of the neck, platysmal bands, become more visible; the condition is sometimes called 'turkey neck.' Wikipedia notes that platysmaplasty and botulinum toxin are the usual interventions, and that facelift surgery and weightlifting may make bands more noticeable. [6]

Botulinum toxin type A enters nerve endings at the neuromuscular junction and cleaves SNAP-25, a protein required for release of acetylcholine, so the muscle receives less signal and relaxes. Recovery occurs as the nerve terminal regenerates its release machinery. [13] Cosmetic effects typically appear within several days and are reported to last roughly two to four months for glabellar lines, with repeat treatment used to maintain results. [13]

Because the platysma pulls the jaw margin and lower face downward, the Nefertiti-lift technique is proposed to release that pull so that the lower face is lifted slightly and the jawline appears more defined. [2][1]

Cosmetic botulinum toxin products are prescription medicines in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and the European Union. In 2002 the FDA approved Botox Cosmetic for glabellar lines; use in the neck is off-label, meaning it is a clinician's practice choice rather than a labelled indication. [13] The FDA added boxed warnings in 2009 about toxin spread from the injection site. [13]

Bruising at injection sites and headache are among the commonly reported cosmetic effects, and weakness in nearby muscles can occur. Wikipedia lists trouble swallowing, headache and unintended weakness of nearby muscles among cosmetic toxin side effects, and notes that masseter injections can reduce the ability to chew solid food. [13]

Human studies include Levy's 2007 report,[2] the 2017 abobotulinumtoxinA study on efficacy and patient selection,[3] a 2018 crossover trial comparing microbotox with the Nefertiti lift,[4] and a registered trial of botulinum toxin for neck rejuvenation in 30 participants.[11] A 2026 split-face study in The Laryngoscope examines jawline contour.[5] Results in detail are not reported in the listings reviewed; consensus reports and reviews also describe the approach.[9][10][12]
No looksmaxxing forum or influencer material was available for this entry. The procedure is included in the wiki as a hardmaxx option for neck bands and jawline definition.

timeline.event: Phillip M. Levy publishes the Nefertiti lift in the Journal of Cosmetic and Laser Therapy.[2]
French paper describes botulinum toxin techniques for the lower face, neck and decollete, including the Nefertiti lift.[8]
Study assesses efficacy and patient selection for neck rejuvenation with botulinum toxin.[3]
Crossover study compares microbotox with the Nefertiti lift.[4]
Split-face study of jawline contour published in The Laryngoscope.[5]
The FDA approves Botox Cosmetic for glabellar lines, establishing cosmetic botulinum toxin use in the US. [13]
